Vignette: Fatima, Age 55

Fatima remembers the exact weight of the bag she carried when she left Syria. Twenty-two pounds. She had weighed it on her kitchen scale before walking out the door of the home she had lived in for thirty years, because some part of her mind - even then, even in the chaos - needed to hold onto something precise and knowable. That was eleven years ago. She has not stopped carrying the weight since.

The journey from Aleppo through Turkey and eventually to the United States took fourteen months and moved through a series of camps, border crossings, and waiting rooms that blur together in her memory like a fever. What does not blur is the night at the Turkish border when the group she was traveling with was stopped by armed men, when her younger sister was separated from her in the dark and not found until three days later. Fatima does not talk about those three days easily. When she does, she describes them as a hole - not a gap in memory, but a place she fell into and has never fully climbed out of.

Her sister survived. Fatima arrived in the United States, eventually settled in a mid-sized Midwestern city, and rebuilt a life with the particular ferocity of someone who has lost everything once and refuses to lose it again. She completed a vocational certification program and became an HVAC technician, a trade she chose deliberately because it requires her to move, to solve problems with her hands, to be useful in a way that is immediate and concrete. She is good at her work. Her colleagues describe her as meticulous, even relentless. What they do not see is that she schedules her service calls in the early morning and avoids jobs in large residential complexes where she might have to work in enclosed basement spaces for extended periods. On the days she cannot avoid it, she finishes the job and then sits in her truck for twenty minutes with the windows down, breathing.

Fatima lives alone. Her marriage ended five years ago, not dramatically, but through a long erosion that she describes with a kind of tired clarity - she could not let anyone close enough to stay, and eventually her husband stopped trying. She has two adult children who call regularly. She loves them in a way that feels desperate to her, a love laced with the constant low-level fear that something will take them from her. She checks her phone compulsively when they do not respond within an hour. She has driven to her daughter's apartment at midnight over a delayed text.

Sleep is where the past finds her most reliably. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart already racing before she is fully conscious, the border crossing replaying not as a memory but as a present-tense emergency. She keeps the lights in her apartment on timers so that no room is ever fully dark when she wakes. She has arranged her furniture so that her bed faces the door. These are not choices she made consciously at first - she noticed them only when her daughter visited and asked why the apartment felt like someone was always ready to leave.

During the day, Fatima moves through the world with a vigilance that exhausts her. Loud sounds - a car backfiring, a door slamming on a job site - pull her out of the present in a way she cannot control. She describes it as being yanked backward by a rope tied around her chest. Crowds make her scan exits. She does not sit with her back to a room.

What weighs on her most, she says, is not the fear itself but the loneliness of it. She has built a life. She has a job she is proud of, children she adores, a small apartment she has made into something that looks like home. And yet some part of her, she says quietly, is still standing at that border in the dark, waiting to find out if her sister is alive.
